title: Brent at $117 While Gulf Physical Crude Sells at a $10 Discount: The Paper Market and the Cargo Market Have Split
subhead: Futures hit a five-month high on escalation fears while Basrah Medium trades at its widest discount to Dubai in months and Gulf exports recover past 81% of prewar levels. Meanwhile Russian diesel sails to New York, EU gas hits 2022 levels, and the US SPR sits at its lowest since 1982.

sections.heading: Two Prices for the Same Barrel
sections.body:
Brent settled the week near $116.70 and WTI around $103.30, with Brent gaining roughly $6 a barrel on the week, per OilPrice pricing. But the physical market underneath has gone the other way. Iraq's Basrah Medium was sold at a discount of about $10 a barrel to the Dubai benchmark, down from near parity a month ago, traders told Bloomberg. The premium of Oman crude over Dubai, the region's key measure of physical strength, fell to its lowest since the end of July.

The reason is volume. Middle Eastern producers have accelerated shuttle-shipping through Hormuz and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, and crude keeps flowing. Citi, cited by OilPrice, estimates Gulf crude exports outside Iran recovered to more than 81% of prewar levels in September, helped by higher Saudi loadings. More than 1 million barrels a day of Gulf crude moved in ship-to-ship transfers in September, about 7.5% of regional exports — a practice that was effectively nonexistent before February.

So the futures curve is pricing a war that might escalate, and the physical market is pricing cargoes that are actually arriving. Both are rational. They are just answering different questions.
sections.whyItMatters: This split is the most useful signal in the market right now. If physical differentials stay weak while futures stay high, refiners with access to Gulf cargoes are printing margin, and the risk premium is increasingly a financial position rather than a supply fact. If the differentials snap back to a premium, the supply picture has actually broken.

sections.heading: The Freight Bill Is Where the War Actually Lives
sections.body:
Citi's point is not that supply is fine — it's that getting crude out of the Gulf and getting it to buyers at a reasonable cost are different problems. VLCC rates from the Gulf to China recently approached $250 per metric ton, roughly $35 a barrel, more than twenty times the previous decade's average, per the bank's estimate carried by OilPrice.

That is the mechanism by which a partly-open strait still produces 2022 prices. The strait handles maybe a fifth of world oil and LNG in normal times; it is not handling a fifth now, but it is handling enough that tankers move — at a price. Citi has spent the year walking back a $60-65 Brent call it made in July, lifting forecasts in August, and now declining to give a target at all, warning that the recovery has been in volumes, not in shipping efficiency.

The knock-on is visible in refined products. US average diesel stood at $6.32 a gallon on October 23, versus $3.63 on the same date last year, according to AAA data cited by OilPrice. Diesel is the fuel that moves trucks, trains, and harvests.
sections.whyItMatters: A war that raises freight by 20x is a tax on every importer regardless of who wins the shooting war. It also explains why India, Japan, and the UK are all now grappling with consumer-level energy politics rather than just procurement.

sections.heading: Russian Diesel Arrives in New York, Weeks After the Deal and Days After the Election Deadline Slips
sections.body:
The tanker Agioi Fanendes, Maltese-flagged, left Russia's Baltic port of Primorsk on Friday carrying about 40,000 metric tons, roughly 300,000 barrels of ultra-low sulfur diesel, bound for New York with an expected arrival of November 7, per shipping data reported by Reuters and OilPrice.

The cargo stems from the Trump-Putin arrangement announced October 9, under which Trump said Russia would ship more than 300,000 tons immediately, 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons thereafter. Moscow partially lifted its own diesel export ban effective October 10, allowing 500,000 tons onto the world market in a first stage, Kommersant reported. The timing is awkward for Washington: the first cargo misses the November 3 midterms by four days, and analysts quoted by OilPrice note the volume is too small to move a tight global diesel market anyway.

The pattern of destinations is the more interesting detail. Vessel tracking cited by Reuters shows other Russian diesel cargoes signaling Turkey and Brazil — the two markets that absorbed Russian product after the EU banned Russian refined products in early 2023. The US is now joining that customer list.
sections.whyItMatters: A US president buying diesel directly from Moscow, while separately pressing Ukraine and sanctioning Russian oil firms, is a real policy contradiction — and it tells you how badly the diesel market is straining. It also quietly legitimizes Russia as a swing supplier of refined product to the Atlantic basin.

sections.heading: Europe's Gas Hits December 2022 Levels With Storage at 75%
sections.body:
TTF, the Dutch benchmark, jumped 3% at the Amsterdam open on Friday to $103.40 (92.30 euros) per megawatt-hour — over $30 per MMBtu — its highest since December 2022, when Europe faced its first winter without most Russian pipeline gas, per OilPrice.

Two things are driving it. Qatari LNG flows remain restricted by the Middle East conflict, and Europe is drawing on storage early as temperatures fall. EU storage stood at 74.62% full on October 22, per Gas Infrastructure Europe data, against a five-year average of about 86% for this point in the year. ING's Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey wrote that European storage 'appears to have peaked at just under 75% full' and that LNG flows are 'increasingly likely to be largely absent from the market for at least much of the Northern Hemisphere winter.'

The UK is a useful stress test. Its grid operator NESO said in its early winter outlook that there is no risk of power or gas outages, projecting a 5.5 GW surplus and an 8.8% buffer over expected peak demand between October 31 and March 31, noting January as the most vulnerable month. But UK front-month gas and electricity prices are up 180% and 120% respectively since February, per Reuters — security of supply and affordability have decoupled.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe enters winter with the least cushion since 2022 and no Qatari baseload in sight. Physical security looks intact for now; the political problem is price, and that is what will drive EU intervention — including, as OilPrice notes, Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen's proposal to delay methane rules on energy imports.

sections.heading: The SPR at 282.7 Million Barrels Is Borrowing a Day and a Half of Crude
sections.body:
The Department of Energy authorized an emergency exchange of up to 400,000 barrels to Phillips 66's Lake Charles refinery in Louisiana on Friday, citing a temporary disruption to crude deliveries, OilPrice reported. Lake Charles runs about 264,000 bpd, so the loan covers roughly a day and a half of throughput. DOE did not say what caused the disruption; Phillips 66 confirmed the receipt and said it expects no operational impact.

The number that matters is the total. The SPR now holds 282.7 million barrels, its lowest since 1982 — a level some analysts describe as the operational minimum. This is the second emergency exchange this month: on October 10, DOE authorized up to 4 million barrels for ExxonMobil and BP after weather-related disruptions. The reserve has been drained by withdrawals during the Iran war and, before that, after Russia's 2022 invasion.

The structure of the transaction is worth noting: it is an exchange, not a sale, and Phillips 66 must return the barrels plus a premium.
sections.whyItMatters: The US buffer that historically capped price spikes is close to unusable. That removes an important psychological anchor from the market and it means Washington's main tools in a further escalation are now releases that barely register, diplomacy, or demand destruction.

sections.heading: Canada Doubles LNG Capacity as Asia Rewires Away From the Gulf
sections.body:
Shell, PETRONAS, PetroChina, Mitsubishi and KOGAS formally approved the FID for LNG Canada Phase 2, doubling the Kitimat facility's capacity to 28 mtpa. With Cedar LNG and Woodfibre under construction, Canada is projected to export 33 mtpa by the end of the decade, per Enerdata and OilPrice.

The geography is the product. Cargoes from British Columbia reach Tokyo in 8-9 days, against 16-18 days from the US Gulf Coast, per S&P Global — and they never transit Hormuz or the Panama Canal. Wood Mackenzie projects Asian LNG demand doubling from about 260 mtpa today to roughly 500 mtpa by 2060, while warning Canada faces a narrowing window as US and other projects accelerate. The demand shift is already measurable: US LNG shipments to Asia more than doubled (+108%) in the first half of 2026 versus the same period in 2025, per EIA data, as buyers scrambled for non-Middle Eastern cargoes.

On the crude side, Chevron secured one year of exclusive negotiation rights to take over operatorship of Iraq's West Qurna 2 field from Russia's Lukoil, following US sanctions on Russian firms, reportedly via a $200 million advance on a prospective signing bonus. OilPrice reports the field could double output to 800,000 bpd.
sections.whyItMatters: Two different de-risking moves in the same week: buyers are signing long-term contracts on routes that avoid the Gulf, and Washington is using sanctions to swap a Russian operator for an American one in Iraq. Both take years to pay off, which is precisely why they are happening now — the current crisis has made the political case for them.

sections.heading: India Drills Its Own Gas, and Iran's Hardliners Talk About the Bomb
sections.body:
State explorer Oil India reported a gas discovery at the Godavari-1 appraisal well in the Matsyapuri formation of the shallow Krishna-Godavari Basin off India's east coast, with a peak test flow of 200,000 standard cubic meters per day, per PTI and OilPrice. The company did not disclose a reserve estimate. India is the world's third-largest crude importer and launched a National Offshore Exploration Scheme this year with $8.8 billion in government support through FY2030-31.

Separately, RFE/RL reporting carried by OilPrice details an unusual shift in Tehran: sitting lawmakers and security officials are now openly arguing for a nuclear weapon. Ahmad Bakhshayesh Ardestani, a member of parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy committee, has argued Iran has already paid the price for its program and should produce weapons. Washington is reportedly weighing strikes on Pickaxe Mountain, the deep underground site where US and Israeli officials say Iran has moved thousands of centrifuges. Trump rejected Iran's proposal for a seven-day ceasefire and phased Hormuz reopening; Vice President JD Vance has said any deal must include a 'meaningful' reduction in Iranian enrichment capacity.
sections.whyItMatters: Iran's public nuclear debate is a negotiating signal as much as a doctrinal shift — it raises the cost of continued bombing and gives Tehran something to trade. For oil markets it means the war has no natural off-ramp in the coming weeks, which is why the futures curve is not following the physical market down.

bottomLine: The striking thing about Friday's market was the gap between the futures tape and the cargo market: Brent near $117 on escalation fears while Basrah Medium sells at a $10 discount to Dubai and Gulf exports run above 81% of prewar levels. The war's real cost is now expressed in freight — $35 a barrel on the Gulf-China route, more than twenty times the historical norm — and in refined products, with US diesel at $6.32 a gallon. Washington's response has been improvisation: a US-bound Russian diesel cargo that arrives four days after the midterms, and a 400,000-barrel SPR loan to one Louisiana refinery while the reserve sits at 282.7 million barrels, the lowest since 1982. Europe enters winter at 75% storage and TTF at 2022 levels, while Canada and India spend the same week building the supply routes that assume the Gulf stays unreliable. Nothing resolved; the hedges are just getting more expensive.
sources: OilPrice.com, Bloomberg, Reuters, Citi, ING (Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey), Gas Infrastructure Europe, Kommersant, S&P Global, Wood Mackenzie, EIA, Enerdata, NESO, AAA, PTI, RFE/RL, Eurasianet
